title: Keep work running after logout
goal: Distinguish hangup resistance, logout survival and a new shell's empty job table.
challenge: Demonstrate protected versus ordinary owned tasks under controlled hangup conditions, then verify a protected task survives console logout. Save and re-check process identities, explain the new job table, and clean up. Reboot and disk Resume must not be claimed to preserve jobs. Equivalent demonstrations are welcome.

steps.explanation: Create guest-local files for PID records and output. No host folder is shared.
steps.expected: The directory exists inside this disposable guest.

steps.explanation: Enable Bash hangup-on-exit only in this interactive login shell. This image normally has it off; ordinary background jobs can survive default logout too.
steps.expected: The output says shopt -s huponexit. Do not edit any shell startup or system policy file.

steps.explanation: nohup makes the command ignore HUP. & backgrounds it; all three standard streams are explicitly handled.
steps.expected: A bounded sleep starts. The log may be empty because sleep prints nothing.

steps.explanation: Immediately record this protected process's PID for the next login.
steps.expected: The file contains its actual PID; this is evidence to inspect, not a permanent identity guarantee.
The current job is this newest task.

steps.explanation: Record it and tell Bash not to send HUP to this job. disown -h does not itself make a new terminal/session.
steps.expected: The job remains listed, but is excluded from Bash's hangup-on-exit signaling.

steps.explanation: Inspect all three before logout and record their arguments.
steps.expected: They are running. Use actual identities, not a fixed job number.

steps.explanation: Log out of the guest shell, not close QEMU. tty1 returns to console-only learner autologin.
steps.expected: A new login prompt/session appears automatically; the VM stays running.

steps.explanation: Inspect the new shell. The previous setting was shell-local.
steps.expected: huponexit is off again and this shell's job table is empty, even when processes survived.

steps.explanation: Read the saved PID and verify the process's owner and arguments again.
steps.expected: The nohup-protected sleep remains. A parent change after logout is normal.

steps.explanation: Compare the ordinary task under the explicitly enabled huponexit experiment.
steps.expected: Normally only the header remains: that ordinary job received HUP and ended.
That task also remains in this pinned image. This is not a universal guarantee against session-manager cleanup.

steps.explanation: After verifying both identities, finish the remaining practice tasks.
steps.expected: The tasks terminate. They are no longer children of the new shell, so wait cannot reap them here.

hints: nohup does not background a task; & is separate. Redirect input/output and save the PID before logout.
Default logout here can leave ordinary jobs alive. The temporary huponexit setting creates a controlled comparison.
After logout use ps, not jobs, to find survivors. Resume disk and reboot start a new kernel and cannot preserve processes.
review: I distinguished default logout behavior from controlled HUP behavior.
I verified a protected process after logout using saved identity evidence.
I explained nohup versus disown, shell-local jobs and shell-local huponexit.
I cleaned up and do not claim survival across reboot or disk Resume.
coverage: Real guest practice; completion is self-reviewed, with no guest assessment or verification score. Partial LPIC-1 103.5 coverage.
